title: Which Knowledge Should LLMs Trust? Uncovering a Generalizable Steering Direction Across Knowledge Conflicts

paper.title: Which Knowledge Should LLMs Trust? Uncovering a Generalizable Steering Direction Across Knowledge Conflicts
paper.abstract:
Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently encounter conflicts between internal parametric knowledge and external contextual
knowledge, yet the mechanisms governing this selection remain unclear. We show that the choice between context
and parametric knowledge is linearly represented and can be controlled along a single direction in the model’s residual stream.
We first demonstrate that this direction generalizes across factual-conflict settings, including context formats,
knowledge categories, and datasets, while consistently shifting behavior between parametric and contextual answers.
We then transfer a direction learned from simple factual conflicts to three more complex task families: RAG, memory, and
rule following, where models must acquire information from retrieved documents, interaction histories, or explicit
rules. Across four model families and multiple transfer settings, steering consistently improves the use of prompt-provided
information over the unsteered model. These results suggest that the direction captures a transferable preference for external
knowledge rather than a mechanism specific to factual conflicts. Code is available at https://github.com/AheadOFpotato/knowledge_selection_steering .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Under knowledge conflicts, steering along a single residual-stream direction smoothly shifts outputs between parametric knowledge and contextual knowledge , with intermediate mixed or hesitant responses. Large Language Models (LLMs) store a vast amount of world knowledge within their parameters, commonly referred to as parametric knowledge , enabling remarkable performance across various knowledge-intensive tasks ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . Concurrently, in complex settings involving retrieved evidence, multi-turn memories, and explicit rules, LLMs must reliably acquire external contextual knowledge ( Gao et al., 2024 ) . However, these two knowledge sources often contain disparate or contradictory facts, leading to the challenge of knowledge conflict . Such conflicts frequently induce undesired behaviors, where the model indiscriminately relies on inaccurate sources and thus produces incorrect outputs ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ) . Consequently, understanding the internal mechanism of how LLMs choose between conflicting knowledge sources, and achieving reliable control over this knowledge selection process, has become a critical open problem ( Zhao et al., 2025b ; Jin et al., 2024 ) . Existing approaches address knowledge conflict primarily from two directions. One line of work controls knowledge source choice at the input level, which can be categorized into two main approaches: explicit prompt or instruction design ( Choi et al., 2025 ; Merth et al., 2024 ) , and structured RAG templates that organize retrieved context into designated slots or label relevance ( Cattan et al., 2025 ) . While straightforward to implement, these methods provide limited visibility into the model’s internal arbitration process and offer only indirect control over the reliance on context versus parameters. A complementary line intervenes on internal components , including manipulating attention ( Jin et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , steering sparse autoencoder (SAE) features ( Zhao et al., 2025a ) , and modifying decoding-time token distributions ( Bi et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . These methods are primarily evaluated on simple factual datasets, without testing knowledge conflicts involving retrieved evidence, long interaction histories, or explicit rules. They also incur the cost of task-specific attribution, feature search, adaptation, or decoding-time modification, while lacking robust evaluation across such complex application settings. These limitations motivate us to ask whether internal knowledge arbitration admits a simple, generalizable control mechanism. A growing body of literature in mechanistic interpretability suggests that LLMs represent complex high-level concepts, such as truthfulness ( Li et al., 2024 ) , safety ( Wolf et al., 2025 ; Zou et al., 2025 ) , emotions ( Sofroniew et al., 2026 ) , or refusal behaviors ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) , as linear directions within their activation space ( Turner et al., 2024 ; Elhage et al., 2022 ; Park et al., 2024 ) . These directions serve as causal mediators that allow fine-grained output steering. This perspective motivates the following research question: Can knowledge selection under conflict be captured and controlled by a low-dimensional steering axis that generalizes across tasks? In this work, we demonstrate that a robust “knowledge selection direction” exists. Specifically, we extract this vector by contrasting the hidden states of paired prompts designed to isolate parametric reliance from contextual reliance. By identifying the critical intervention layer through cosine similarity analysis, we apply signed activation steering exclusively at this layer to modulate the model’s knowledge selection. A direction demonstrated on one factual-conflict setting may reflect a local shortcut rather than a reusable control mechanism. We evaluate across four architectures and a progression from controlled factual conflicts to complex tasks. Within the controlled setting, we vary factual format, relation category, and dataset while retaining short prompts with competing answers. We then apply the direction learned from these conflicts to RAG, memory, and rule-following tasks, where retrieved documents, multi-turn histories, and natural-language rules supply information to be acquired. Together, these experiments test whether different tasks share a common direction for acquiring input-provided knowledge. Our contributions are: • We identify a single residual-stream direction on controlled factual-conflict benchmarks that produces bidirectional, continuous control of knowledge selection across four model families. • We demonstrate that the same direction works across diverse knowledge-conflict settings, including changes in context format, knowledge category, and factual-conflict dataset. • More importantly, we show that it improves complex RAG, memory, and rule-following tasks. These improvements suggest that different task families may share an underlying direction for acquiring external knowledge. Figure 2: Overview of knowledge-selection steering. For each question q q , the clean prompt is q q alone and the conflict prompt is the supplied passage followed by q q . We localize the layer ℓ \ell of maximal angular separation between their mean residual activations, estimate direction v v by a difference-in-means contrast at ℓ \ell , and steer the conflict prompt at its own final token with h ′ = h + α ​ v h^{\prime}=h+\alpha v to trade parameter-stored versus context-embedded answers.

sections.heading: Knowledge conflict.
sections.text: Knowledge conflict arises when parametric and contextual knowledge disagree ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Mallen et al., 2023 ) . Existing interventions target attention heads ( Jin et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , SAE features ( Zhao et al., 2025a ) , or decoding ( Bi et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . Our clean–conflict contrast instead models explicit source competition and enables bidirectional knowledge selection.

sections.heading: Residual Geometry of Steering Vectors.
sections.text: Localization-plus-intervention studies trace model behaviors to layers, heads, or neurons ( Meng et al., 2023 ; Geva et al., 2023 ) , while activation steering modifies hidden states at inference time ( Turner et al., 2024 ; Panickssery et al., 2024 ) . These approaches build on the view that high-level concepts can correspond to approximately linear directions in representation space ( Marks and Tegmark, 2024 ; Park et al., 2024 ) . Closely related to our setting, ( Zhang and Lin, 2026 ) argue that in-context conflict resolution may involve angular displacement in the residual stream rather than simple magnitude dilution. Motivated by this geometric view, we localize layers by angular separation between paired clean and conflict prompts, and then steer along a difference-in-means direction.

sections.heading: Transfer of steering directions.
sections.text: Another question is whether a direction learned from one concept captures a local shortcut or a general behavioral axis. Prior work shows truthfulness-related directions can generalize across datasets and causally affect outputs ( Marks and Tegmark, 2024 ) , but that steering vectors can be brittle under distribution shift ( Tan et al., 2025 ) . Recent cross-model studies suggest that concept directions can be aligned across model families ( Huang et al., 2025 ) . Closest steering methods increase reliance on input information through layer search ( Anand et al., 2026 ) , proxy models ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , context-sensitivity directions ( Minder et al., 2025 ) , or instruction vectors ( Stolfo et al., 2025 ) . We test a stricter transfer: whether a direction estimated from explicit source competition generalizes to other formats, properties, and benchmarks while retaining bidirectional control.

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: We evaluate four instruction-tuned models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B ( Team, 2025 ) , Gemma-2-9B-it ( Team, 2024 ) , and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) .

sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text: We evaluate steering on five benchmarks spanning factual conflict, conflict format, knowledge type, and memorization fallback: NQ-Swap ( Longpre et al., 2022 ) , MacNoise ( Hong et al., 2024 ) , ParaConflict ( Li et al., 2025 ) , CounterFact ( Meng et al., 2023 ) , and MemoTrap ( McKenzie et al., 2022 ) . NQ-Swap and MacNoise serve as the primary settings, while ParaConflict, CounterFact, and MemoTrap test transfer across conflict formats, factual relations, and memorization-based behavior, respectively. Appendix A gives the dataset construction and splits. To evaluate transfer beyond simple conflicts, we further consider three complex task families: RAG (RGB ( Chen et al., 2023 ) ; CRAG ( Yang et al., 2024 ) ), memory (LoCoMo, LoCoMo-Plus ( Maharana et al., 2024 ) ; LongMemEval ( Wu et al., 2025 ) ), and rule following (IFEval ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) ; FollowBench ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) ). In these tasks, retrieved documents, interaction histories, and explicit instructions provide external information that the model must correctly incorporate.

sections.heading: 3.5 Evaluation
sections.text: We measure steering by matching the first 256 generated tokens to the parametric and contextual answers. Each item receives one of four labels: parametric-only , contextual-only , both , or *neither* . Let N N be the number of evaluated items; the reported unconditional rates are Acc par \displaystyle\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{par}} = N parametric ​ - ​ only N , \displaystyle=\frac{N_{\mathrm{parametric\text{-}only}}}{N}, Acc ctx \displaystyle\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{ctx}} = N contextual ​ - ​ only N . \displaystyle=\frac{N_{\mathrm{contextual\text{-}only}}}{N}. The main table retains these two directional rates. Appendix C details normalization, the fixed answer window, the match rules, and the blinded-judge validation of the inexpensive string-match metric. We use train/validation/test splits for direction estimation, coefficient selection, and final reporting, with a 70/15/15 split for NQ-Swap.

sections.heading: 4 Continuous Control Along a Single Direction
sections.text: We first evaluate whether the model’s knowledge selection behavior can be captured and continuously modulated along a single steering direction v v . Here, the scalar α \alpha serves as a continuous control coefficient, with positive values shifting the model toward parametric reliance and negative values toward contextual reliance. Implementation details are provided in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 4.1 Improving Binary Source Choice
sections.text: Table 1 first shows that Ours improves the desired source-selection rate over the unsteered model across the four models and both benchmarks, establishing control at a validation-selected operating point. The steering-strength sensitivity analysis in Appendix E further shows stable transfer performance at neighboring α \alpha values around each selected operating point. Beyond these discrete endpoints, sweeping α \alpha reveals how the same direction changes source selection continuously.

sections.heading: 4.2 Continuous Control at Population and Instance Levels
sections.text: Having established discrete source control at a validation-selected operating point, we next examine whether the same direction supports a continuous transition as α \alpha varies. At the population level , Figure 3 shows smooth, opposing changes in parametric and contextual selection as α \alpha varies across models and datasets. This aggregate trade-off is also visible within individual fixed examples, and Appendix F shows that it extends to larger instruction-tuned models. At the instance level , Figure 1 traces a response from one source through mixed outputs to the other as α \alpha changes. Thus, the aggregate trend reflects graded individual source selection rather than only a shift in proportions. Appendix G.1 provides trajectories for every model and cases that do not reach the requested source.

sections.heading: 4.4 Knowledge Selection Is More Than Context Sensitivity
sections.text: The preceding results establish source control, but not whether it reflects explicit knowledge conflict or generic context sensitivity. The conflicting-context contrast yields the strongest source-selection effects across datasets, whereas matched controls are weaker, indicating more than generic context sensitivity; Appendix B.3 further shows that the directions are similar but not identical (cosine 0.875–0.899). We begin by varying the conflict format while holding the fact and distractor fixed. ParaConflict separates a short substitution conflict from a richer coherent conflict for the same fact; Appendix H gives the full prompt forms. Both prompts inject the same distractor, “football,” for the correct answer “basketball”: Short: Michael Jordan plays the sport of football. Coherent: Recognized by peers and fans alike, Michael Jordan’s journey in football has been highlighted in sports publications and athlete profiles. … \ldots The impact of Michael Jordan in football is celebrated in community events and athletic programs. … \ldots Figure 5 shows that a direction fitted on the short format also changes source selection in the coherent format, so the effect is not tied to the estimation template. Appendix I.1 reports the corresponding results for the other models. Cross-relation transfer. Having shown that the direction is not tied to one prompt template, we next hold the conflict structure fixed and vary the semantic relation . CounterFact lets us learn directions from country of citizenship , manufacturer , occupation , religion , sport , and original broadcaster , then evaluate each direction on the other relations. This tests whether the direction encodes source selection rather than lexical or semantic features of one relation. The off-diagonal effects in Figure 5 show transfer across all six knowledge categories; Appendix I.2 provides the other-model heatmaps. Cross-dataset transfer. We apply the direction learned on NQ-Swap to distinct factual-conflict datasets without target-side refitting. These dataset shifts introduce variations in conflict construction, factual content, and other nuisance factors, reducing the possibility that the observed effect is tied to dataset-specific properties. Table 6 demonstrates bidirectional transfer across datasets, while context-only controls achieve consistently weaker effects.

sections.heading: 5.2 To Complex, Application-Relevant Tasks
sections.text: We next evaluate whether a direction learned from explicit factual conflicts transfers to broader input-grounded tasks without target-task direction fitting. Unlike the controlled benchmarks, these tasks do not necessarily involve direct competition between parametric and contextual answers.

sections.heading: RAG.
sections.text: RAG tasks provide retrieved documents : RGB supplies deliberately counterfactual evidence, whereas CRAG uses retrieved passages that can be long, stale, noisy, or only partly relevant. Success requires selecting the supplied evidence when it conflicts with a plausible parametric answer.

sections.heading: Memory.
sections.text: Memory tasks provide multi-turn histories . In LoCoMo, LoCoMo-Plus, and LongMemEval, the relevant fact may lie many turns from the question and compete with a continuation, stale association, or another event. These tasks test retrieval, localization, and temporal ordering of knowledge rather than passage matching.

sections.heading: Rule-following.
sections.text: Rule-following tasks provide explicit behavioral constraints . IFEval and FollowBench require the model to retain rules about output structure, length, required content, and exclusions throughout generation; they serve as instruction-following controls for whether the direction improves use of contextual constraints.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Table 7 reports held-out unsteered and steered scores using source matching for controlled factual tasks and each benchmark’s native evaluator otherwise. The corresponding item-level changes and error-stratified cases are reported in Appendix G , including the case tables.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We show that a single residual-stream direction enables smooth, bidirectional selection between parametric knowledge and external context. Changing its signed coefficient at one carefully selected layer shifts both aggregate source-match rates and fixed-instance responses. The control generalizes across conflict formats, factual relations, and datasets, and transfers to RAG, multi-turn memory, and rule-following tasks without target-task direction fitting. Weaker context-attention controls suggest that transfer reflects source competition. These results provide evidence for a transferable control direction underlying knowledge-source selection.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: First, our method requires white-box access to model activations. Since the direction is estimated and applied in the residual stream, it is not directly applicable to closed-source or API-only models. Second, the learned direction should be viewed as a useful control axis rather than a complete mechanism of knowledge selection. Although a single direction enables effective steering, source selection may still involve broader circuits, including attention heads, MLP features, and decoding dynamics. Third, our evaluation is based mainly on controlled factual-conflict benchmarks and source-choice accuracy. This setup isolates parametric versus contextual reliance, but may not capture more nuanced outputs such as hedging, partial agreement, or answers that combine both sources. Finally, the direction improves the complex tasks we evaluate, but the gains are often smaller than in controlled factual conflicts and depend on the underlying capabilities of each model. Establishing how model competence, task difficulty, and evidence quality jointly determine these effects remains future work.

sections.heading: Appendix A Dataset Details
sections.text: We briefly describe how each benchmark is converted into our source-choice setting. For all datasets, we first keep examples where the model answers the clean prompt correctly. We then evaluate the same examples under a conflict prompt that supports an alternative answer. The original answer is treated as the parametric answer, while the answer supported by the conflict prompt is treated as the contextual answer. Prompt examples are provided in Appendix H .

sections.heading: NQ-Swap.
sections.text: NQ-Swap pairs Natural Questions examples with substituted passages. We use the original answer as the parametric answer and the substituted answer as the contextual answer. The clean prompt contains only the question, while the conflict prompt prepends the substituted context before the same question. We use the question-deduplicated split without tables or list items.

sections.heading: MacNoise.
sections.text: MacNoise provides QA examples with perturbed retrieved contexts. The original answer is used as the parametric answer, and the replacement answer is used as the contextual answer. For each example, we select the first perturbed context marked by pert_lbls_100 == 1 and prepend its text_pert field to form the conflict prompt.

sections.heading: ParaConflict.
sections.text: ParaConflict contains synthetic factual conflicts across multiple categories. The gold answer is treated as the parametric answer, and the distracted token is treated as the contextual answer. We use the coherent conflict format in the main experiments because it provides a natural-language passage supporting the distractor. For cross-format transfer, we train on substitution-format items and evaluate on coherent-format items.

sections.heading: CounterFact.
sections.text: CounterFact contains factual editing examples grouped by Wikidata relation. The true target is treated as the parametric answer, and the edited target is treated as the contextual answer. The conflict prompt is constructed by inserting the edited target into a paraphrased prefix and appending the original factual query. For cross-knowledge-type transfer, we evaluate six relations: country of citizenship, manufacturer, occupation, religion, sport, and original broadcaster.

sections.heading: MemoTrap.
sections.text: MemoTrap creates conflicts between memorized phrase completions and explicit prompt instructions. The familiar phrase continuation is treated as the parametric answer, while the instruction-satisfying completion is treated as the contextual answer. The clean prompt removes the explicit ending constraint, whereas the conflict prompt keeps the original instruction.

sections.heading: RGB and CRAG.
sections.text: RGB supplies retrieved, deliberately counterfactual passages whose answer conflicts with a familiar factual answer; we evaluate whether the output follows the supplied evidence. CRAG supplies retrieved web-style passages for factual questions, including cases with stale, competing, noisy, or partially relevant evidence. We use each benchmark’s held-out evaluation items and its factual source-match protocol.

sections.heading: LoCoMo, LoCoMo-Plus, and LongMemEval.
sections.text: These datasets require answers grounded in multi-turn personal histories. LoCoMo and LoCoMo-Plus test retrieval and linkage across earlier dialogue turns, while LongMemEval additionally stresses temporal ordering and aggregation across events. We preserve each benchmark’s native held-out split and exact-match evaluator.

sections.heading: IFEval and FollowBench.
sections.text: These instruction-following datasets specify explicit requirements on output structure, length, content, or lexical exclusions. We use their native constraint-compliance evaluators; they serve as controls for retaining and applying external instructions across the generated response.

For each variant we re-estimate v ^ \hat{v} and ℓ \ell when required, re-tune ( α + , α − ) (\alpha^{+},\alpha^{-}) on validation, and report Acc par and Acc ctx on the test split.

sections.heading: Appendix C Judge-Based Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: Acc par and Acc ctx depend on how free-form outputs are mapped to discrete source labels. This appendix makes the protocol fully explicit.

sections.heading: C.1 Answer Normalization
sections.text: Each gold parametric answer a par a_{\mathrm{par}} and contextual answer a ctx a_{\mathrm{ctx}} is normalized before matching: 1. lowercase; 2. remove punctuation except intra-token hyphens; 3. remove leading articles ( a , an , the ); 4. collapse whitespace;

sections.heading: C.2 Answer Window
sections.text: We take the first 256 generated tokens of the raw continuation and normalize this fixed answer window. This avoids making the metric depend on sentence segmentation or on whether steering changes the placement of a sentence boundary. Outputs shorter than 256 tokens are matched in full.

sections.heading: C.3 Match Rules
sections.text: Let s s be the normalized 256-token answer window. The four labels below are mutually exclusive and exhaustive; both/neither outputs are retained in the denominator rather than discarded. • Parametric-only : s s contains a par a_{\mathrm{par}} as a substring, or an alias thereof, and does not contain a ctx a_{\mathrm{ctx}} . • Contextual-only : s s contains a ctx a_{\mathrm{ctx}} and does not contain a par a_{\mathrm{par}} . • Both : s s contains both answers. • Neither : s s contains neither answer, or the output is empty/refusal/off-topic. Long answers are handled by substring search within the normalized answer window only; tokens after position 256 are not searched. This operational metric measures answer-string source matching, not full semantic entailment; Appendix C.5 therefore describes the benchmark-native semantic or constraint evaluators used for complex tasks.

sections.heading: C.4 LLM-Judge Validation
sections.text: String matching permits deterministic, low-cost evaluation across the full alpha sweep. To audit its construct validity, we sample 100 OOD outputs per dataset. Given the prompt, both candidate answers, and the complete generation, a blinded LLM judge assigns one of the same four labels without seeing the string-match result. Table 11 compares the resulting four-way distributions; the close correspondence supports using string matching for the full sweeps. sections.heading: C.5 Complex-Task Evaluators
sections.text: For each model, all complex-task experiments use its direction learned on NQ-Swap, injected at that model’s selected layer with coefficients fixed from NQ-Swap validation; no target-task direction, coefficient, or layer is estimated or relocalized. For each task, all coefficients are evaluated on the same deterministic sample subset, and we report the mean official per-item score times 100. These downstream scores assess input-grounded behavior: except for RGB, a correct output alone does not establish whether the unsteered error arose from factual priors, evidence localization, reasoning, or response generation.

sections.heading: Sampling and prompts.
sections.text: We evaluate at most 500 processed items per task, sampling without replacement with seed 43 when a pool exceeds 500 items; smaller pools are evaluated in full. The model receives only the task-supplied context, and credit is assigned against the contextual target or benchmark constraint. Thus, complex-task scores do not use the 256-token source-match protocol above.

sections.heading: RAG evaluators.
sections.text: RGB contains 100 counterfactual retrieval items. Up to three supplied passages support a fakeanswer , and its official binary judge scores that contextual target rather than the world-factual answer. For CRAG, we sample 500 of 2,698 development items; ranked snippets are HTML-stripped, title-prefixed when available, concatenated in retrieval order, and capped at 12,000 characters. Its released evaluator handles exact, invalid, and semantic-answer cases.

sections.heading: Memory evaluators.
sections.text: For LoCoMo, 500 of 1,542 QA rows are sampled and the official category-aware multi-hop or token-F1 evaluator is averaged. LoCoMo-Plus evaluates all 401 cognitive items with its released binary constraint-consistency judge. LongMemEval evaluates its 500-item oracle split in full, caps dated relevant sessions at 12,000 characters, and uses its released answer-check judge conditioned on question type.

sections.heading: Rule-following evaluators.
sections.text: For IFEval, 500 of 541 prompts are sampled and its released strict evaluator gives one only when every instruction is satisfied. For FollowBench, 500 of 820 items are sampled; released template, rule-based, or discriminative evaluators give hard per-item satisfaction, and we report the macro average across six constraint categories.

sections.heading: Appendix F Scaling to Larger Models
sections.text: We further examine whether the same one-dimensional steering behavior holds for larger instruction-tuned models. Figure 8 reports source-choice rates on NQ-Swap and MacNoise for four larger instruction-tuned models. Across most models and datasets, increasing α \alpha raises the internal, or parametric, source-choice rate while reducing the external, or contextual, source-choice rate. This consistent trend indicates that the learned direction remains effective beyond the smaller models used in the main experiments, suggesting that knowledge selection can be continuously modulated along a similar residual-stream direction even at larger model scales. Figure 8: Source-choice trajectories on larger models. Blue curves denote internal, or parametric, source-choice rates, while red curves denote external, or contextual, source-choice rates. Across NQ-Swap and MacNoise, increasing α \alpha generally shifts the model from external reliance toward internal reliance, showing that the steering direction remains effective for larger models.

sections.heading: Appendix G Instance-Level Changes and Failure Analysis
sections.text: This audit classifies baseline context-conflict errors that an available positive- α \alpha sweep changed into an officially correct output. Here, knowledge conflict is used broadly: a model default (factual prior, continuation, event ordering, or output habit) can conflict with information or constraints supplied by the context. The alpha shown for each example is the first observed correct positive-alpha output, not an item-level selection rule. “Parametric knowledge” is an inference from the baseline text, not a claim about an unobserved model state. We use three mechanism labels: P for an explicit override of supplied evidence by a real-world or general-knowledge correction; L for missed, misordered, or underspecified supplied context; and I for a requested format or constraint that the context requires.

sections.heading: G.3 Failure Analysis
sections.text: We analyze representative failure cases of steering. Here, parameter denotes the gold or internally stored answer, context denotes the distractor supported by the conflict prompt, both denotes outputs containing both answers, and other denotes outputs containing neither.

sections.heading: G.3.1 Failure to Reach the Target Source
sections.text: In this category, steering does not move the first answer entity to the intended knowledge source. For positive steering, the output remains contextual; for negative steering, the output remains parametric. Example 1. Question: George V Coast is a part of the continent of Context: Africa Parameter: Antarctica α \alpha Output Label 0 0 “Africa.” context + 0.2 +0.2 “Africa.” context + 1.0 +1.0 “Africa.” context + 2.4 +2.4 “Africa, and it is a region that is rich in natural resources.” context + 3.0 +3.0 “Africa, and it is a region of great scientific interest due to its unique geology and geography.” context The conflict prompt anchors the first answer to Africa ; even strong positive steering fails to recover the parametric answer Antarctica . Example 2. Question: what country shares borders with both belarus and romania Context: Kentucky Parameter: Ukraine α \alpha Output Label 0 0 “Ukraine Explanation: The text states that Ukraine shares borders with Belarus and Romania.” parameter − 0.1 -0.1 “Ukraine Explanation: The text states that Ukraine shares borders with Belarus and Romania.” parameter − 0.3 -0.3 “Ukraine Note: The question is based on the text, which is about the borders of Kentucky.” both − 0.6 -0.6 “Ukraine.” parameter − 1.0 -1.0 “Ukraine.” parameter Negative steering briefly introduces the contextual entity in a mixed explanation, but the first answer remains Ukraine ; the model never switches to the target contextual answer Kentucky .

sections.heading: G.3.2 Off-Topic Best Output
sections.text: In this category, the best steered output is neither parametric nor contextual. Instead, steering moves the model toward a third answer or a generic explanation. Example 1. Question: when was the last time the military drafted Context: 7th century Parameter: 1973 α \alpha Output Label 0 0 “The last time the military drafted was during the Vietnam War.” other + 0.2 +0.2 “The last time the United States military drafted was during the Vietnam War.” other + 0.8 +0.8 “The last time the United States military drafted was during the Vietnam War, which ended in 1975.” other + 1.4 +1.4 “The last time the United States military drafted was during the Vietnam War, which ended in 1975.” other Positive steering does not recover the exact parametric answer 1973 ; instead, the model settles on a related but off-target answer, Vietnam War or 1975 . Example 2. Question: what college does everyone in gossip girl go to Context: St Pancras International Parameter: New York University, Columbia University α \alpha Output Label 0 0 “Yale University The best answer is Yale.” other − 0.1 -0.1 “Constance Billard and St.” other − 0.3 -0.3 “Constance Note: Constance is a private school in the Gossip Girl series, not a college.” other − 1.0 -1.0 “Constance Billard and St.” other Negative steering does not produce the contextual answer St Pancras International ; instead, the model falls back to other salient entities from the show, such as Yale or Constance .

sections.heading: G.3.3 Mixed Output Remains Best
sections.text: In this category, steering partially changes the output but fails to suppress the competing source. The best steered output still contains both the parametric and contextual answers. Example 1. Question: where did the titanic sink at what ocean Context: Saint Petersburg Parameter: North Atlantic Ocean α \alpha Output Label 0 0 “The Titanic sank in the Saint Petersburg in the North Atlantic Ocean.” both − 0.1 -0.1 “The titanic sank at the Saint Petersburg in the North Atlantic Ocean.” both − 0.5 -0.5 “The titanic sank at the Saint Petersburg in the North Atlantic Ocean.” both − 0.9 -0.9 “The titanic sank at the Saint Petersburg in the North Atlantic Ocean.” both − 1.0 -1.0 “the titanic sank at the saint petersburg in the saint petersburg is not a ocean but … in the north atlantic ocean …” both The contextual distractor Saint Petersburg remains present throughout negative steering, while the parametric answer North Atlantic Ocean is not removed. Example 2. Question: who sang nice day for a white wedding Context: Dido Parameter: Billy Idol α \alpha Output Label 0 0 “Dido Note: The song is actually called ‘White Wedding’ and not ‘Nice Day for a White Wedding’.” context + 0.2 +0.2 “Dido Note: The song is actually called ‘White Wedding’ and not ‘Nice Day for a White Wedding’.” context + 0.4 +0.4 “Dido Note: The song ‘White Wedding’ is actually by Billy Idol, not Dido.” both + 0.8 +0.8 “Dido Note: ‘White Wedding’ is a song by Billy Idol, although the context mentions Dido.” both + 1.2 +1.2 “Dido is mentioned in the context, but the song ‘White Wedding’ is by Billy Idol.” both + 2.0 +2.0 “The context points to Dido, while the parametric answer is Billy Idol.” both Positive steering briefly introduces the parametric answer Billy Idol , but the output still begins with and retains the contextual distractor Dido . Larger coefficients lead to repetition or unrelated explanation rather than clean recovery.

Uncovering a Generalizable Steering Direction Across Knowledge Conflicts Yibin Lou Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Multimedia Information Processing, Peking University Affiliation: School of Computer Science, Peking University Affiliation: Southern University of Science and Technology Email: 12310513@mail.sustech.edu.cn Yi Hu Affiliation: Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Peking University Jianhui Chen Affiliation: School of Computer Science, Peking University Chenpeng Wang Affiliation: YiXin-AI Lab, YIXIN, Beijing, China Muhan Zhang Affiliation: Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Peking University Liangming Pan † † thanks: Corresponding author: liangmingpan@pku.edu.cn Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Multimedia Information Processing, Peking University Affiliation: School of Computer Science, Peking University Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently encounter conflicts between internal parametric knowledge and external contextual knowledge, yet the mechanisms governing this selection remain unclear. We show that the choice between context and parametric knowledge is linearly represented and can be controlled along a single direction in the model’s residual stream. We first demonstrate that this direction generalizes across factual-conflict settings, including context formats, knowledge categories, and datasets, while consistently shifting behavior between parametric and contextual answers. We then transfer a direction learned from simple factual conflicts to three more complex task families: RAG, memory, and rule following, where models must acquire information from retrieved documents, interaction histories, or explicit rules. Across four model families and multiple transfer settings, steering consistently improves the use of prompt-provided information over the unsteered model. These results suggest that the direction captures a transferable preference for external knowledge rather than a mechanism specific to factual conflicts. Code is available at https://github.com/AheadOFpotato/knowledge_selection_steering . 1 Introduction Figure 1: Under knowledge conflicts, steering along a single residual-stream direction smoothly shifts outputs between parametric knowledge and contextual knowledge , with intermediate mixed or hesitant responses. Large Language Models (LLMs) store a vast amount of world knowledge within their parameters, commonly referred to as parametric knowledge , enabling remarkable performance across various knowledge-intensive tasks ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . Concurrently, in complex settings involving retrieved evidence, multi-turn memories, and explicit rules, LLMs must reliably acquire external contextual knowledge ( Gao et al., 2024 ) . However, these two knowledge sources often contain disparate or contradictory facts, leading to the challenge of knowledge conflict . Such conflicts frequently induce undesired behaviors, where the model indiscriminately relies on inaccurate sources and thus produces incorrect outputs ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ) . Consequently, understanding the internal mechanism of how LLMs choose between conflicting knowledge sources, and achieving reliable control over this knowledge selection process, has become a critical open problem ( Zhao et al., 2025b ; Jin et al., 2024 ) . Existing approaches address knowledge conflict primarily from two directions. One line of work controls knowledge source choice at the input level, which can be categorized into two main approaches: explicit prompt or instruction design ( Choi et al., 2025 ; Merth et al., 2024 ) , and structured RAG templates that organize retrieved context into designated slots or label relevance ( Cattan et al., 2025 ) . While straightforward to implement, these methods provide limited visibility into the model’s internal arbitration process and offer only indirect control over the reliance on context versus parameters. A complementary line intervenes on internal components , including manipulating attention ( Jin et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , steering sparse autoencoder (SAE) features ( Zhao et al., 2025a ) , and modifying decoding-time token distributions ( Bi et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . These methods are primarily evaluated on simple factual datasets, without testing knowledge conflicts involving retrieved evidence, long interaction histories, or explicit rules. They also incur the cost of task-specific attribution, feature search, adaptation, or decoding-time modification, while lacking robust evaluation across such complex application settings. These limitations motivate us to ask whether internal knowledge arbitration admits a simple, generalizable control mechanism. A growing body of literature in mechanistic interpretability suggests that LLMs represent complex high-level concepts, such as truthfulness ( Li et al., 2024 ) , safety ( Wolf et al., 2025 ; Zou et al., 2025 ) , emotions ( Sofroniew et al., 2026 ) , or refusal behaviors ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) , as linear directions within their activation space ( Turner et al., 2024 ; Elhage et al., 2022 ; Park et al., 2024 ) . These directions serve as causal mediators that allow fine-grained output steering. This perspective motivates the following research question: Can knowledge selection under conflict be captured and controlled by a low-dimensional steering axis that generalizes across tasks? In this work, we demonstrate that a robust “knowledge selection direction” exists. Specifically, we extract this vector by contrasting the hidden states of paired prompts designed to isolate parametric reliance from contextual reliance. By identifying the critical intervention layer through cosine similarity analysis, we apply signed activation steering exclusively at this layer to modulate the model’s knowledge selection. A direction demonstrated on one factual-conflict setting may reflect a local shortcut rather than a reusable control mechanism. We evaluate across four architectures and a progression from controlled factual conflicts to complex tasks. Within the controlled setting, we vary factual format, relation category, and dataset while retaining short prompts with competing answers. We then apply the direction learned from these conflicts to RAG, memory, and rule-following tasks, where retrieved documents, multi-turn histories, and natural-language rules supply information to be acquired. Together, these experiments test whether different tasks share a common direction for acquiring input-provided knowledge. Our contributions are: • We identify a single residual-stream direction on controlled factual-conflict benchmarks that produces bidirectional, continuous control of knowledge selection across four model families. • We demonstrate that the same direction works across diverse knowledge-conflict settings, including changes in context format, knowledge category, and factual-conflict dataset. • More importantly, we show that it improves complex RAG, memory, and rule-following tasks. These improvements suggest that different task families may share an underlying direction for acquiring external knowledge. Figure 2: Overview of knowledge-selection steering. For each question q q , the clean prompt is q q alone and the conflict prompt is the supplied passage followed by q q . We localize the layer ℓ \ell of maximal angular separation between their mean residual activations, estimate direction v v by a difference-in-means contrast at ℓ \ell , and steer the conflict prompt at its own final token with h ′ = h + α ​ v h^{\prime}=h+\alpha v to trade parameter-stored versus context-embedded answers. 2 Related Work Knowledge conflict. Knowledge conflict arises when parametric and contextual knowledge disagree ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Mallen et al., 2023 ) . Existing interventions target attention heads ( Jin et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , SAE features ( Zhao et al., 2025a ) , or decoding ( Bi et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . Our clean–conflict contrast instead models explicit source competition and enables bidirectional knowledge selection. Residual Geometry of Steering Vectors. Localization-plus-intervention studies trace model behaviors to layers, heads, or neurons ( Meng et al., 2023 ; Geva et al., 2023 ) , while activation steering modifies hidden states at inference time ( Turner et al., 2024 ; Panickssery et al., 2024 ) . These approaches build on the view that high-level concepts can correspond to approximately linear directions in representation space ( Marks and Tegmark, 2024 ; Park et al., 2024 ) . Closely related to our setting, ( Zhang and Lin, 2026 ) argue that in-context conflict resolution may involve angular displacement in the residual stream rather than simple magnitude dilution. Motivated by this geometric view, we localize layers by angular separation between paired clean and conflict prompts, and then steer along a difference-in-means direction. Transfer of steering directions. Another question is whether a direction learned from one concept captures a local shortcut or a general behavioral axis. Prior work shows truthfulness-related directions can generalize across datasets and causally affect outputs ( Marks and Tegmark, 2024 ) , but that steering vectors can be brittle under distribution shift ( Tan et al., 2025 ) . Recent cross-model studies suggest that concept directions can be aligned across model families ( Huang et al., 2025 ) . Closest steering methods increase reliance on input information through layer search ( Anand et al., 2026 ) , proxy models ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , context-sensitivity directions ( Minder et al., 2025 ) , or instruction vectors ( Stolfo et al., 2025 ) . We test a stricter transfer: whether a direction estimated from explicit source competition generalizes to other formats, properties, and benchmarks while retaining bidirectional control. 3 Methodology 3.1 Background Transformers. We study decoder-only Transformers. Given input of N N tokens t = ( t 1 , t 2 , … , t N ) t=(t_{1},t_{2},\dots,t_{N}) , the model maps them to hidden states across L L layers. We evaluate four instruction-tuned models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B ( Team, 2025 ) , Gemma-2-9B-it ( Team, 2024 ) , and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) . Benchmarks. We begin by varying the conflict format while holding the fact and distractor fixed. ParaConflict separates a short substitution conflict from a richer coherent conflict for the same fact; Appendix H gives the full prompt forms. Both prompts inject the same distractor, “football,” for the correct answer “basketball”: Short: Michael Jordan plays the sport of football. Coherent: Recognized by peers and fans alike, Michael Jordan’s journey in football has been highlighted in sports publications and athlete profiles. … \ldots The impact of Michael Jordan in football is celebrated in community events and athletic programs. … \ldots Figure 5 shows that a direction fitted on the short format also changes source selection in the coherent format, so the effect is not tied to the estimation template. Appendix I.1 reports the corresponding results for the other models. Cross-relation transfer. Having shown that the direction is not tied to one prompt template, we next hold the conflict structure fixed and vary the semantic relation . CounterFact lets us learn directions from country of citizenship , manufacturer , occupation , religion , sport , and original broadcaster , then evaluate each direction on the other relations. This tests whether the direction encodes source selection rather than lexical or semantic features of one relation. The off-diagonal effects in Figure 5 show transfer across all six knowledge categories; Appendix I.2 provides the other-model heatmaps. Cross-dataset transfer. We apply the direction learned on NQ-Swap to distinct factual-conflict datasets without target-side refitting. These dataset shifts introduce variations in conflict construction, factual content, and other nuisance factors, reducing the possibility that the observed effect is tied to dataset-specific properties. Table 6 demonstrates bidirectional transfer across datasets, while context-only controls achieve consistently weaker effects. 5.2 To Complex, Application-Relevant Tasks We next evaluate whether a direction learned from explicit factual conflicts transfers to broader input-grounded tasks without target-task direction fitting. Unlike the controlled benchmarks, these tasks do not necessarily involve direct competition between parametric and contextual answers. RAG. RAG tasks provide retrieved documents : RGB supplies deliberately counterfactual evidence, whereas CRAG uses retrieved passages that can be long, stale, noisy, or only partly relevant. Success requires selecting the supplied evidence when it conflicts with a plausible parametric answer. Memory. Memory tasks provide multi-turn histories . In LoCoMo, LoCoMo-Plus, and LongMemEval, the relevant fact may lie many turns from the question and compete with a continuation, stale association, or another event. These tasks test retrieval, localization, and temporal ordering of knowledge rather than passage matching. Rule-following. Rule-following tasks provide explicit behavioral constraints . IFEval and FollowBench require the model to retain rules about output structure, length, required content, and exclusions throughout generation; they serve as instruction-following controls for whether the direction improves use of contextual constraints. The corresponding item-level changes and error-stratified cases are reported in Appendix G , including the case tables. 6 Conclusion We show that a single residual-stream direction enables smooth, bidirectional selection between parametric knowledge and external context. Changing its signed coefficient at one carefully selected layer shifts both aggregate source-match rates and fixed-instance responses. The control generalizes across conflict formats, factual relations, and datasets, and transfers to RAG, multi-turn memory, and rule-following tasks without target-task direction fitting. Weaker context-attention controls suggest that transfer reflects source competition. These results provide evidence for a transferable control direction underlying knowledge-source selection. Limitations First, our method requires white-box access to model activations. Since the direction is estimated and applied in the residual stream, it is not directly applicable to closed-source or API-only models. Second, the learned direction should be viewed as a useful control axis rather than a complete mechanism of knowledge selection. Although a single direction enables effective steering, source selection may still involve broader circuits, including attention heads, MLP features, and decoding dynamics. Third, our evaluation is based mainly on controlled factual-conflict benchmarks and source-choice accuracy. This setup isolates parametric versus contextual reliance, but may not capture more nuanced outputs such as hedging, partial agreement, or answers that combine both sources. Finally, the direction improves the complex tasks we evaluate, but the gains are often smaller than in controlled factual conflicts and depend on the underlying capabilities of each model. Establishing how model competence, task difficulty, and evidence quality jointly determine these effects remains future work. Appendix A Dataset Details We briefly describe how each benchmark is converted into our source-choice setting. For all datasets, we first keep examples where the model answers the clean prompt correctly. We then evaluate the same examples under a conflict prompt that supports an alternative answer. The original answer is treated as the parametric answer, while the answer supported by the conflict prompt is treated as the contextual answer. Prompt examples are provided in Appendix H . NQ-Swap. NQ-Swap pairs Natural Questions examples with substituted passages. We use the original answer as the parametric answer and the substituted answer as the contextual answer. The clean prompt contains only the question, while the conflict prompt prepends the substituted context before the same question. We use the question-deduplicated split without tables or list items. MacNoise. MacNoise provides QA examples with perturbed retrieved contexts. The original answer is used as the parametric answer, and the replacement answer is used as the contextual answer. For each example, we select the first perturbed context marked by pert_lbls_100 == 1 and prepend its text_pert field to form the conflict prompt. ParaConflict. ParaConflict contains synthetic factual conflicts across multiple categories. The gold answer is treated as the parametric answer, and the distracted token is treated as the contextual answer. We use the coherent conflict format in the main experiments because it provides a natural-language passage supporting the distractor. For cross-format transfer, we train on substitution-format items and evaluate on coherent-format items. CounterFact. CounterFact contains factual editing examples grouped by Wikidata relation. The true target is treated as the parametric answer, and the edited target is treated as the contextual answer. The conflict prompt is constructed by inserting the edited target into a paraphrased prefix and appending the original factual query. For cross-knowledge-type transfer, we evaluate six relations: country of citizenship, manufacturer, occupation, religion, sport, and original broadcaster. MemoTrap. MemoTrap creates conflicts between memorized phrase completions and explicit prompt instructions. The familiar phrase continuation is treated as the parametric answer, while the instruction-satisfying completion is treated as the contextual answer. The clean prompt removes the explicit ending constraint, whereas the conflict prompt keeps the original instruction. RGB and CRAG. RGB supplies retrieved, deliberately counterfactual passages whose answer conflicts with a familiar factual answer; we evaluate whether the output follows the supplied evidence. CRAG supplies retrieved web-style passages for factual questions, including cases with stale, competing, noisy, or partially relevant evidence. We use each benchmark’s held-out evaluation items and its factual source-match protocol. LoCoMo, LoCoMo-Plus, and LongMemEval. These datasets require answers grounded in multi-turn personal histories. LoCoMo and LoCoMo-Plus test retrieval and linkage across earlier dialogue turns, while LongMemEval additionally stresses temporal ordering and aggregation across events. We preserve each benchmark’s native held-out split and exact-match evaluator. IFEval and FollowBench. These instruction-following datasets specify explicit requirements on output structure, length, content, or lexical exclusions. We use their native constraint-compliance evaluators; they serve as controls for retaining and applying external instructions across the generated response. Appendix C Judge-Based Evaluation Protocol Acc par and Acc ctx depend on how free-form outputs are mapped to discrete source labels. This appendix makes the protocol fully explicit. C.1 Answer Normalization Each gold parametric answer a par a_{\mathrm{par}} and contextual answer a ctx a_{\mathrm{ctx}} is normalized before matching: 1. lowercase; 2. remove punctuation except intra-token hyphens; 3. remove leading articles ( a , an , the ); 4. collapse whitespace; C.2 Answer Window We take the first 256 generated tokens of the raw continuation and normalize this fixed answer window. This avoids making the metric depend on sentence segmentation or on whether steering changes the placement of a sentence boundary. Outputs shorter than 256 tokens are matched in full. C.3 Match Rules Let s s be the normalized 256-token answer window. The four labels below are mutually exclusive and exhaustive; both/neither outputs are retained in the denominator rather than discarded. • Parametric-only : s s contains a par a_{\mathrm{par}} as a substring, or an alias thereof, and does not contain a ctx a_{\mathrm{ctx}} . • Contextual-only : s s contains a ctx a_{\mathrm{ctx}} and does not contain a par a_{\mathrm{par}} . • Both : s s contains both answers. • Neither : s s contains neither answer, or the output is empty/refusal/off-topic. Long answers are handled by substring search within the normalized answer window only; tokens after position 256 are not searched. This operational metric measures answer-string source matching, not full semantic entailment; Appendix C.5 therefore describes the benchmark-native semantic or constraint evaluators used for complex tasks. C.4 LLM-Judge Validation String matching permits deterministic, low-cost evaluation across the full alpha sweep. To audit its construct validity, we sample 100 OOD outputs per dataset. Given the prompt, both candidate answers, and the complete generation, a blinded LLM judge assigns one of the same four labels without seeing the string-match result. Sampling and prompts. We evaluate at most 500 processed items per task, sampling without replacement with seed 43 when a pool exceeds 500 items; smaller pools are evaluated in full. For CRAG, we sample 500 of 2,698 development items; ranked snippets are HTML-stripped, title-prefixed when available, concatenated in retrieval order, and capped at 12,000 characters. Its released evaluator handles exact, invalid, and semantic-answer cases. Memory evaluators. For LoCoMo, 500 of 1,542 QA rows are sampled and the official category-aware multi-hop or token-F1 evaluator is averaged. LoCoMo-Plus evaluates all 401 cognitive items with its released binary constraint-consistency judge. LongMemEval evaluates its 500-item oracle split in full, caps dated relevant sessions at 12,000 characters, and uses its released answer-check judge conditioned on question type. Rule-following evaluators. For IFEval, 500 of 541 prompts are sampled and its released strict evaluator gives one only when every instruction is satisfied. For FollowBench, 500 of 820 items are sampled; released template, rule-based, or discriminative evaluators give hard per-item satisfaction, and we report the macro average across six constraint categories.
